snippet.description:

The episode highlights the complex interplay between conquest, propaganda, and cultural assimilation in the ancient Mediterranean world.

snippet.title: The Fall of Carthage: How Rome Erased a Superpower
snippet.description:
The fall of Carthage was one of the most devastating turning points in ancient history. In this video, we explore how Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BC at the end of the Third Punic War, ending one of the Mediterranean’s greatest powers forever.

This historical reconstruction covers the rise of Carthage, the legacy of Hannibal, Roman fear after the Punic Wars, the siege of Carthage, Scipio Aemilianus, and the final destruction of the city. Built in a cinematic 2D animation style, this video aims to present the story in a dramatic but historically grounded way.

Topics covered in this video:

* Carthage and the Punic Wars
* Hannibal and Rome’s long memory
* Why Rome wanted Carthage destroyed
* The Third Punic War
* The siege and fall of Carthage
* What historians say about the destruction of the city

After a three-year siege by Roman legions in the Third Punic War, the defenders of Carthage, the capital of the Carthaginian Empire, were on the verge of capitulation.

This film provides an immersive ambient experience that acoustically and visually transports the viewer into the dramatic events that led to the fall of the once mighty Punic metropolis and its defeat against the Roman Empire.

Ambient sounds and atmospheric images give you the feeling of actually floating above Carthage. Dive into the times of the Roman Republic and experience history up close.

snippet.title: Carthage Must be Destroyed - Third Punic War (Part 1) DOCUMENTARY
snippet.description:
Documentary on the Third Punic War between Rome and Carthage! Part 2: https://youtu.be/vyJmLGtM5Eo Get started with career coaching for your own projects with today's sponsor https://strawberry.me/invicta

In part 1 of this series we set the stage for the final climactic showdown between Rome and Carthage. This involves a recap of the preceding First Punic War and Second Punic War which had ultimately seen the Romans emerge victorious. We then see how both sides navigated their way through the following interbellum years. For Carthage this largely meant upheavals at home as it attempted to stave off internal and external pressures. For Rome meanwhile this largely meant a continuation of its campaigns to dominate the Mediterranean.

We then take a closer look at the spark of war which was ignited by the opportunistic attacks of the Numidian King Massinissa against his neighbor. In such matters, Rome refused to play the impartial arbiter. Such a situation proved untenable for Carthage which was eventually forced to take matters into its own hands to defend itself. However this would have grave consequences when the Roman Senate not leapt at the opportunity to declare war. A showdown a monumental proportions looms on the horizon.

Stay tuned as we prepare to cover the siege of Carthage in full detail.

snippet.title: History of Ancient Carthage | Short-Animated Documentary
snippet.description:
Ancient Carthage, founded by Phoenician colonists in the 9th century BC, evolved into a dominant empire stretching across the Mediterranean. Boasting economic prowess and a powerful navy, Carthage engaged in rivalries, notably with the Greek city-state of Syracuse, marked by political intrigue and military conflict. Despite the resilience of both sides during the Sicilian Wars, Carthage gradually asserted control over much of the western Mediterranean.

The pinnacle of Carthage's rivalry came with Rome during the Punic Wars, a series of conflicts spanning from 264 BC to 146 BC. These wars, fought over trade routes and territorial dominance, saw Rome emerge victorious, culminating in the sacking and eventual destruction of Carthage. Despite its demise, Carthage's cultural identity, rooted in its Canaanite heritage and marked by commercial acumen and unique governance, left a lasting impact on ancient civilization.

Reflecting Phoenician traditions, Carthaginian society contributed innovations such as serial production and the cothon harbor, while its system of government combined elements of democracy, oligarchy, and republicanism. Despite the destruction of much of its history, modern archaeological research offers nuanced insights into Carthaginian civilization, challenging historical narratives and enriching our understanding of this ancient powerhouse.

snippet.description:
The story of Carthage’s final days is not just about war — it’s about pride, vengeance, and the cost of victory.
A century after Hannibal’s defeat, Rome returned to finish what it started. Under Scipio Aemilianus, the Roman legions surrounded Carthage — once the richest city in the world — and vowed to erase it from history.

For three long years, Carthage resisted. Women turned their hair into ropes for catapults. Children carried stones to the walls. But when the final Roman assault came, the city burned for six days and nights. Even as the flames consumed temples and homes, the people refused to surrender.

In the end, Carthage fell, its land salted, its people enslaved, and its name turned into a warning for all time.
Rome had achieved its final victory — but at the cost of its humanity.

“There will come a day when Rome shall fall, as Carthage has fallen.”
– Scipio Aemilianus

snippet.title: Genocide in the Ancient World (Documentary) (Destruction of Carthage) (Siege of Melos)
snippet.description:
Genocide is often viewed as a particular feature of our own current age. This perception largely stems from the terrible events which took place during World War Two in the 20th century CE in the parts of Europe occupied by the Nazis. However, there are certain occasions in the ancient world which could also be possibly considered as genocide. In considering genocide from an historical perspective, it is necessary to firstly ask what exactly is genocide? The concept is one which most people can agree did happen but which remains very hard to define precisely.

The word itself was first coined in 1944 CE by the Polish writer Raphael Lemkin (1900-1959) who constructed the word by combining ‘geno-’, from the Greek word for race or tribe, with ‘-cide’, from the Latin word for killing. The modern notion of genocide owes a great deal to Lemkin’s work who developed his ideas during his youth in Eastern Europe and as a resistance fighter against the German army during World War Two (Elder 2005; McDonnell and Moses 2005). In his key work published in 1944 CE, Axis Rule in Occupied Europe, Lemkin described genocide as signifying ‘a coordinated plan of different actions aiming at the destruction of essential foundations of the life of national groups, with the aim of annihilating the groups themselves’ (Jones 2006: 10-11). The second most influential document in laying out the modern legal notion of genocide was the 1948 United Nations adoption of the ‘Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide’ wherein Article II of the convention defined genocide as the ‘intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group’.

The exact explanation of what constitutes genocide resulting from these two landmark works has been extensively debated by academics ever since. However, it can be observed that there are two main elements needed for an event to be considered as genocide, namely: there is a clear intent on the behalf of the perpetrators to carry out the action and the resulting annihilation of a particular political, social or cultural group. Keeping this in mind, it may be possible to identify two possible cases of genocide in the ancient world: the Roman destruction of Carthage in 146 BCE and the Athenian massacre at Melos in 416 BCE.

Kings and Generals' historical animated documentary series on the history of Rome continues with the episode on the First Punic War. The First Punic War (264–241 BC) was the first great clash between Rome and Carthage, two rising powers of the Mediterranean world. Sparked by disputes in Sicily, the conflict quickly escalated into a brutal struggle for dominance on land and at sea. Rome, a land power with little naval experience, built a fleet from scratch and introduced innovations like the corvus boarding device, turning sea battles into infantry encounters. Carthage, a maritime superpower, relied on its superior navy, seasoned commanders, and alliances with Sicilian cities. Over two decades of grinding warfare, both sides suffered devastating losses from storms, blockades, and costly campaigns. Battles such as Agrigentum, Mylae, and Ecnomus shaped the course of the war, while Rome’s failed invasion of Africa highlighted the enormous risks of expansion. Ultimately, Rome’s resilience and relentless pursuit of victory led to Carthage’s defeat and the signing of a peace treaty in 241 BC. This marked Rome’s first step as a Mediterranean empire and laid the foundation for future clashes in the Second and Third Punic Wars. Join us as we explore the strategies, battles, and consequences of this pivotal conflict in ancient history.

Kings and Generals' historical animated documentary series on the history of Rome continues with the episode on the First Punic War. The First Punic War (264–241 BC) was the first great clash between Rome and Carthage, two rising powers of the Mediterranean world. Sparked by disputes in Sicily, the conflict quickly escalated into a brutal struggle for dominance on land and at sea. Rome, a land power with little naval experience, built a fleet from scratch and introduced innovations like the corvus boarding device, turning sea battles into infantry encounters. Carthage, a maritime superpower, relied on its superior navy, seasoned commanders, and alliances with Sicilian cities. Over two decades of grinding warfare, both sides suffered devastating losses from storms, blockades, and costly campaigns. Battles such as Agrigentum, Mylae, and Ecnomus shaped the course of the war, while Rome’s failed invasion of Africa highlighted the enormous risks of expansion. Ultimately, Rome’s resilience and relentless pursuit of victory led to Carthage’s defeat and the signing of a peace treaty in 241 BC. This marked Rome’s first step as a Mediterranean empire and laid the foundation for future clashes in the Second and Third Punic Wars. Join us as we explore the strategies, battles, and consequences of this pivotal conflict in ancient history.

snippet.title: Ancient Rome's Most Terrifying Victory: Could You Survive the Destruction of Carthage?
snippet.description:
Ancient Rome's Most Terrifying Victory: Could You Survive the Destruction of Carthage?

In 146 BC, one of the most devastating events in ancient history took place when the armies of the Roman Republic destroyed their greatest rival — the powerful North African city of Carthage.

This moment marked the dramatic end of the Third Punic War, a brutal struggle that had lasted years and followed two earlier wars between Rome and Carthage. Roman forces led by Scipio Aemilianus surrounded the city and launched a final assault that would change the Mediterranean world forever.

Ancient historians such as Polybius described a terrifying urban battle lasting several days as Roman troops fought street by street through the city. Fires spread through neighborhoods, buildings collapsed, and thousands of civilians were caught in the chaos.

When the fighting ended, Carthage — once one of the richest and most powerful cities in the ancient world — had been completely destroyed. Survivors were taken into captivity, and the city itself was left in ruins.

The fall of Carthage secured Rome’s dominance over the western Mediterranean and marked a turning point in the rise of Roman imperial power.

This video explores:

The long rivalry between Rome and Carthage

The brutal siege that led to the city’s fall

What ancient historians recorded about the destruction

And how this victory reshaped the ancient world

Step into the final days of Carthage and witness one of the most terrifying victories in Roman history.
